Passion means an extremely strong, intense feeling — one that goes far beyond simple liking or interest. When you feel passion, the feeling is so powerful that it drives your actions, fills your thoughts, and often feels difficult to control. It is not a calm, quiet feeling. It is a feeling that burns.

Passion is used in a few related but distinct ways:

1. A deep love for an activity, subject, or cause

This is the most common meaning in everyday modern use. If you have a passion for something, it means you love it intensely, think about it constantly, and are powerfully driven to pursue it.

"Photography is her passion."
"He has a passion for justice."
"She threw herself into her work with passion."

This kind of passion is not just a hobby or a preference. A hobby is something you enjoy. A passion is something you cannot imagine living without. It consumes you in a good way.

2. Intense romantic love or physical desire

Passion is also used to describe a powerful romantic and physical attraction between people — the kind of love that feels overwhelming, urgent, and deeply emotional, not just affectionate or companionable.

"The passion between them was undeniable."
"Their relationship began with a wild, burning passion."

This is why we call romantic feelings "passionate" when they are fiery and consuming, as opposed to love that is gentle, steady, and calm.

3. Any overwhelming, barely-controlled emotion

In a broader sense, passion refers to any intense emotion — not just love or enthusiasm, but also anger, grief, or excitement — especially when that emotion is so strong it threatens to take over rational thinking.

"In a moment of passion, he said words he could never take back."
"She wept with passion at the loss of her friend."
"The crowd erupted in passion."

Notice how this usage captures emotion at its most raw and overwhelming. The phrase "in a moment of passion" specifically suggests that the emotion was so intense, the person lost some control over their words or actions.

4. The Passion (Christianity — capitalized)

When written with a capital P, The Passion refers specifically to the suffering, crucifixion, and death of Jesus Christ. This is a religious and historical usage you will encounter in Christian texts, music (like Bach's St. Matthew Passion), art, and films. It is a specialized meaning and does not connect to everyday use of the word, though it does reflect the original sense of the word as "suffering" or "enduring great pain."
What Makes Passion Different from Similar Words

Many words describe strong feelings or interest, but passion sits in a specific place among them. Understanding these differences will sharpen your sense of the word:

  • Interest — a mild, calm attraction. You notice something, you are curious. Far less intense than passion.
  • Enthusiasm — strong positive energy and excitement. Closer to passion, but enthusiasm is lighter and more controlled. You can be enthusiastic on a Monday morning. Passion tends to be deeper and longer-lasting.
  • Obsession — like passion in its intensity, but obsession carries a negative feeling. An obsession is unhealthy, intrusive, and hard to escape. Passion is usually seen as admirable and energizing.
  • Desire — wanting something strongly. Passion can include desire, but passion is broader — it also includes love, commitment, and emotional depth.
  • Zeal — strong devotion and enthusiasm, often toward a cause or goal. Very close to passion but slightly more action-focused. Zeal is about pushing forward; passion is more about the feeling itself.
  • Fervour — burning intensity of feeling, very similar to passion. Often used in religious, political, or ideological contexts.
How Passion Feels (and Why It Matters)

One of the defining qualities of passion is that it does not feel like a choice. You do not decide to be passionate about something the way you decide to pick a favourite colour. Passion seems to arrive on its own, and once it is there, it shapes everything. A person with a passion for music does not just listen to music — they think in music, they breathe music, they feel incomplete when away from it.

This is also why passion is closely tied to loss of control. When we say someone acted in a fit of passion, we mean their emotion overwhelmed their reasoning. Courts of law, literature, and everyday speech all recognize this quality of passion — that it has a power that can temporarily override calm thinking.

This is the double-edged nature of passion: it can be the source of your greatest achievements (a musician driven by passion for their craft), and it can also lead to moments of recklessness or regret (words spoken in a passionate argument that cannot be unsaid).

The noun passion is used in several fixed expressions worth knowing:

  • "A passion for [something]" — the standard way to say you are passionate about something.
    "She has a passion for learning."
  • "With passion" — describing how someone does something.
    "He argued with passion."
  • "Passion project" — something you work on not for money or fame, but purely because you love it.
    "His documentary was a passion project, years in the making."
  • "Burning passion" — an intensifier, emphasizing the heat and urgency of the feeling.
    "She felt a burning passion to change the world."
  • "In a moment / fit of passion" — acting driven by overwhelming emotion, often regrettably.
    "She quit her job in a fit of passion and regretted it the next morning."
  • "The passions" (plural, literary/philosophical) — a collective term for all strong human emotions and urges. Found in older literature and philosophy.
    "He struggled to keep his passions in check."

Passion is an intensely powerful feeling — whether it is a deep, driving love for something you do, an overwhelming romantic desire for someone, or any emotion so strong it temporarily overrides your ability to think calmly.
